who: J. Marc Milner, military and naval historian at the University of New Brunswick, PhD UNB.

evidence.says: The history faculty list identifies J. Marc Milner as professor and chair, with BA, MA and PhD from UNB; appointment year 1986.
Marc Milner joined UNB History in 1986 and directed its military and strategic studies program and subsequently the Gregg Centre.
Joseph Milner's authority identifies the author of The history of the church of Christ, cited in an 1809 edition.
John Milner's authority identifies the author of Symbolists and decadents and Vladimir Tatlin and the Russian avant-garde.

notes: Neither candidate matches: p-134762 is the earlier church historian Joseph Milner; p-134050 is the art historian John Milner.

who: Gerald D. Nash, historian of the American West at the University of New Mexico, PhD Berkeley 1957.

evidence.says: Richard Etulain identifies Gerald D. Nash as a UNM historian, with a Berkeley doctorate in American history in 1957 and service at UNM from 1961 to 1995.
The candidate's authority expands his name to Gerald David Nash and identifies him as distinguished professor of history at the University of New Mexico.

notes: Institution, supervisory period, field and doctorate institution/year agree.

who: Joseph Howard Parks, historian of the American South and professor at the University of Georgia.

evidence.says: The authority identifies Joseph Howard Parks, also Joseph H. Parks, as author of General Edmund Kirby Smith, C.S.A., and records that he taught at the University of Georgia.
The publisher credits Joseph Howard Parks with Joseph E. Brown of Georgia and identifies Joseph H. Parks as professor emeritus at the University of Georgia.

notes: The candidate's full name, Georgia affiliation and southern political/Civil War field fit the supervisor and dissertations. The supplied Ohio State doctorate year was not independently verified.

who: Harry A. Miskimin, Yale historian of medieval and early modern economic history, PhD Yale 1960.

evidence.says: The candidate item identifies Harry A. Miskimin, PhD Yale 1960, links LC n50033551, and lists doctoral students H. Clark Johnson, John Peder Maarbjerg and Diane Claire Margolf.
The 1987-1988 visiting-scholar record names Dr. Harry A. Miskimin as the faculty host at Yale University.
The authority identifies Harry A. Miskimin as author of Money, prices, and foreign exchange in fourteenth-century France and The economy of later Renaissance Europe 1460-1600.

notes: The candidate's listed students overlap the AHA group; Yale affiliation in the relevant period and economic-history works corroborate the match.

who: David C. Carter, Auburn historian of civil rights and the modern American South, PhD Duke 2001.

evidence.says: Auburn identifies David C. Carter as a history professor who arrived in 2000, received his Duke PhD in 2001, and studies civil rights and the American South.
This candidate is David John Carter, author of Australian literary and cultural studies, a Melbourne graduate who taught at Griffith and became professor at Queensland.
D. M. Carter is David M. Carter, lecturer in Greek at Reading and author of The politics of Greek tragedy.
David J. Carter is also named David John Carter; the authority associates him with the Alberta legislature and Behind Canadian barbed wire.

notes: All three supplied candidates are different authors. Auburn gives 2001 for the supervisor's Duke doctorate, whereas the AHA input gives 2000.

who: Ken Cruikshank, McMaster historian of Canadian transport and environmental history, PhD York.

evidence.says: McMaster identifies Ken Cruikshank as a history professor who joined in 1993, earned his PhD at York, and authored Close Ties: Railways, Government and the Board of Railway Commissioners, 1851-1933.
The candidate authority identifies Ken Cruikshank as author of Close ties (1991), then an assistant professor of history at Trent.
The faculty association's service-award account gives 1989 for Cruikshank's York PhD and connects his early railway research to Close Ties.

notes: The identical book bridges the authority and McMaster profile; institution, field and York doctorate agree. McMaster's account gives 1989 for the PhD, versus 1988 in the AHA input.

who: William R. Taylor, historian of American cultural history at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the 1960s.

evidence.says: Taylor's January 1967 American History Laboratory Project report identifies him as a Wisconsin history professor in summer 1966 and names Neil Coughlan, Steven Nissenbaum and Donald Scott among Wisconsin graduate participants.
The authority identifies William R. (William Robert) Taylor, author of Cavalier and Yankee, and cites publisher information that he taught at Harvard, Wisconsin, Chicago and Stony Brook.

notes: The candidate's Wisconsin employment is corroborated by his contemporary report, which also names three students from this group.

who: James Kirby Martin, historian of early America and the American Revolution at the University of Houston, PhD Wisconsin.

evidence.says: Houston explicitly names James Kirby Martin as advisor for Phillip Sinitiere, Christopher J. Smith, J. Kent McGaughy, Andrew Walmsley, Karen Guenther and Elizabeth O'Kane Lipartito, with the dissertation titles supplied in the group.
Houston identifies James Kirby Martin as an early American historian who earned his MA and PhD at Wisconsin and taught at Houston from 1980.
The candidate authority identifies James Kirby Martin as author of Men in rebellion (1973).

notes: Direct department evidence establishes the supervisor's full name across all six supplied students, selecting p-106416 from the namesakes.
